optional_codes.reason: New confusion is documented in the history. It is not listed as a diagnosis and the provider does not tie it to the sepsis. It can be read as part of the septic presentation or as a separate symptom. It is not required, and it is accepted if reported. Either answer is defensible.

citations.case: ICD-10-CM Official Guidelines FY2027, Section I.C.1.d.1.a (sepsis: assign the systemic infection code; with no organism identified, the unspecified-organism sepsis code is used); Section I.C.1.d.4 (sepsis with a localized infection: the systemic infection code is sequenced first, the localized infection second); Section I.C.1.d.1.b (severe sepsis requires provider documentation of associated acute organ dysfunction; R65.2- is not assigned from vital signs or lactate alone); Section I.B.5 (signs and symptoms integral to a definitive diagnosis are not coded separately)

coder_notes: The provider documents sepsis due to urinary tract infection. No organism is identified (cultures pending), so the unspecified-organism sepsis code is first-listed, followed by the urinary tract infection, site not specified. Severe sepsis and septic shock are not documented: lactate 3.1, blood pressure 96/58 and new confusion without a provider statement of organ dysfunction are a query opportunity, not a coding decision. New confusion is accepted but not required (see optional_codes). Fever, burning with urination, tachycardia and tachypnea are integral to the diagnoses. Pyuria and positive nitrite are findings that support the urinary tract infection. Bacteremia is not documented. The case is the emergency department encounter; the admission is a separate encounter. Traps: sequencing the urinary tract infection first; assigning R65.20 or R65.21 from the vital signs and lactate; adding a bacteremia or pyuria code; adding an organism code while cultures are pending
